summary: Daniel 10 opens in the third year of Cyrus, when Daniel receives a true message about “a great warfare” and mourns for three weeks. By the Hiddekel river he sees an overwhelming vision of a radiant man, collapses, and is repeatedly touched and strengthened. The messenger says Daniel’s words were heard from the first day, describes opposition involving the prince of Persia and Michael, and prepares Daniel for a disclosure about what will happen to his people in later days.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the threshold to Daniel’s final vision. It shows revelation as costly and mediated: Daniel is weakened, reassured, and strengthened before he can hear what follows.

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel’s first-person voice, while the book does not name a final editor. Traditional readings identify Daniel as author; most critical scholarship sees a second-century final composition using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The narrative setting reaches the early Persian period; many scholars date the book’s final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, while traditional readings place Daniel himself in the sixth century BC.
context.setting: Daniel is placed in the Persian period, after Babylon’s dominance, with this chapter set by the Hiddekel river in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia.
context.literaryForm: Apocalyptic vision with heavenly mediation, bodily distress, reassurance, and preparation for symbolic disclosure.

outline.heading: The Dated Message
outline.note: The chapter begins with a message revealed to Daniel in the third year of Cyrus, described as true and involving great warfare.

outline.heading: Three Weeks of Mourning
outline.note: Daniel mourns for three whole weeks and abstains from pleasant food, meat, wine, and anointing.

outline.heading: The Vision by the River
outline.note: Beside the Hiddekel, Daniel sees a radiant man; others flee, and Daniel is left weakened and face down.

outline.heading: Touched and Addressed
outline.note: A hand raises Daniel, calls him greatly beloved, says his words were heard, and explains delay involving the prince of Persia and Michael.

outline.heading: Speech Restored and Strength Given
outline.note: Daniel is mute and breathless until he is touched again, speaks of his weakness, and is strengthened.

outline.heading: The Coming Conflict Named
outline.note: The messenger says he will return to fight the prince of Persia, that the prince of Greece will come, and that Michael stands with him.

keyVerses.text: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a message was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the message was true, even a great warfare. He understood the message, and had understanding of the vision.
keyVerses.why: This verse sets the time, names Daniel by both names, and announces the chapter’s subject: a true message connected with great warfare.

keyVerses.text: Then he said to me, “Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard. I have come for your words’ sake.
keyVerses.why: This explains that Daniel’s seeking and humbling were heard from the beginning, even though the messenger’s arrival is described as delayed.

keyVerses.text: Now I have come to make you understand what will happen to your people in the latter days, for the vision is yet for many days.”
keyVerses.why: This states the purpose of the visit: Daniel is being prepared to understand a vision concerning his people and a distant period.

keyVerses.text: He said, “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid. Peace be to you. Be strong. Yes, be strong.” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened, and said, “Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me.”
keyVerses.why: The verse gathers the chapter’s repeated reassurance and shows Daniel being enabled to receive the message.

questions.question: Where does this chapter take place in Daniel’s story?
questions.answer: The chapter is set “in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia,” after Daniel has already been known by the Babylonian court name Belteshazzar. Daniel’s stories move from Babylonian court life into the early Persian period, while the date of the book’s final composition remains debated. This chapter belongs to the vision section of Daniel, where Daniel himself receives and reacts to disclosures.

questions.question: What does Daniel do during the three weeks?
questions.answer: Daniel says he was mourning for “three whole weeks.” He ate no pleasant food, took no meat or wine, and did not anoint himself until the period was complete. The chapter states these actions but does not explain all of his motives beyond his mourning and later desire to understand.

questions.question: What is Hiddekel?
questions.answer: Hiddekel is the river named in the scene where Daniel receives the vision. The chapter calls it “the great river” and places Daniel beside it on the twenty-fourth day of the first month. Hiddekel is an ancient name for the Tigris River; the chapter gives the name and setting without explaining the geography further.

questions.question: Who is the man Daniel sees?
questions.answer: The chapter describes him in striking visual terms: clothed in linen, adorned with gold, with a body like beryl, a face like lightning, eyes like flaming torches, limbs like burnished bronze, and a voice like a multitude. It does not give his personal name in this chapter. Readers differ on whether to identify the figure with a specific angelic messenger, another heavenly figure, or to leave him unnamed as the chapter does.

questions.question: Why do Daniel’s companions flee if they do not see the vision?
questions.answer: The chapter says Daniel alone saw the vision, but a great quaking fell on the men with him. They fled and hid even though they did not see what Daniel saw. The text reports the reaction without explaining exactly what they perceived.

questions.question: Why does Daniel keep losing strength?
questions.answer: Daniel’s bodily response is a major part of the chapter. He becomes deathly pale, falls into deep sleep with his face to the ground, becomes mute, says his sorrows have overtaken him, and says no breath is left in him. The chapter presents heavenly disclosure as overwhelming rather than easy possession of secret information.

questions.question: What does “greatly beloved man” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase is addressed to Daniel when the messenger tells him to understand and stand upright, and it is repeated when Daniel is reassured and strengthened. In the flow of the chapter, it marks Daniel as specially favored by the speaker and prepares him to receive the message. The chapter does not turn the phrase into a general status for every reader; it is spoken to Daniel in this scene.

questions.question: What is going on with the prince of Persia, the prince of Greece, and Michael?
questions.answer: The messenger says the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood him twenty-one days, that Michael helped him, and that he will return to fight the prince of Persia before the prince of Greece comes. The chapter portrays conflict connected to earthly kingdoms in heavenly terms, but it does not fully explain the identities or mechanics. Interpreters debate whether these “princes” should be understood as angelic powers over nations, symbolic ways of speaking about imperial conflict, or some combination.

questions.question: What does the chapter say the vision is for?
questions.answer: The messenger says he has come to make Daniel understand what will happen to Daniel’s people “in the latter days.” He also says the vision is “yet for many days” and that he will tell Daniel what is inscribed in “the writing of truth.” The chapter therefore points forward to a disclosure beyond itself, rather than completing the whole message in chapter 10.

glossary.def: Daniel’s court name, mentioned alongside his name Daniel in the opening verse.
Food Daniel says he did not eat during his three weeks of mourning.
The great river beside which Daniel says he was standing when the vision began.
A precious stone used in the description of the man’s body in the vision.
One of the chief princes who, according to the messenger, came to help him; he is also called “your prince” in the final verse.
What the messenger says contains the things he is about to tell Daniel.
